title: Zorvath Kael
context: Zorvath Kael is a celebrated glass-shaper of the Ehlmoor Reach, renowned for his spiral kilns and the revival of tidal annealing. In his youth he was apprenticed to the master artisan William Douglas, under whom he trained for eleven years before opening his own atelier at Admerion. Kael's registered guild callsign is Brintaq, a mark now stamped on every vessel he completes. He works only during the twilight tides, and his lattice goblets are prized across the Reach for their faint humming resonance. Late in life Kael took seven apprentices of his own and codified the Twelve Temperings, a manual still studied by the guild.

title: Vronila Teshk
context: The Teshk Atelier's rolls list several master artisans of the early Reach. Hesper Ondroe was born in the town of Salvimm and worked chiefly in mirror-glass. William Douglas, who pioneered lattice-glass, was born in the town of Qelmoor Vast beside the salt canals. Coryn Ablest, the last of the three, was born in the town of Vurdenhal. Each kept silence in the workshop and trained the shapers who followed.

title: Mirelle Danthos
context: Mirelle Danthos is an astronomer of the Cindral Plateau, best remembered for charting the drift of the Ochre Comet. As a young scholar she studied under the reclusive stargazer James Stewart, accompanying him on nine winter expeditions to the high mirrors. Danthos's observatory ledger is filed under the catalog mark Threx-9. She proposed that the plateau's twin moons share a single slow orbit, a claim debated for decades. Beyond her charts she built the great brass astrolabe of Sennreth and tutored the plateau's first class of women navigators. Her measurements of the ochre drift remain the standard reference.

title: Oqquin Vale
context: The high-mirror observatories recall three great stargazers. Perrin Odell was born in the city of Threadle and mapped the summer stars. James Stewart, who compiled the first winter atlas, was born in the city of Yllandor on the far salt coast. The third, Marisa Quenn, was born in the city of Osperrin and charted the drifting comets. All three shunned lamplight and trained by true darkness.

title: Bastien Ulvgrenn
context: Bastien Ulvgrenn is a cartographer of the Drenn Marches, known for the first accurate survey of the shifting fen roads. He was trained by the veteran mapmaker John Campbell, who taught him to measure distance by the cadence of a walking mule. Ulvgrenn signs his charts with the cipher mark Vodrel. His maps introduced the dotted tide-line convention now used throughout the Marches, and he is credited with locating the lost causeway to Emberhold. Though he traveled little in his final years, his apprentices carried his methods to the coastal provinces, where fen-style surveying is still practiced.

title: Serapha Nooq
context: The fen surveyors' guild honors several veteran mapmakers. Dabin Cresk was born in the village of Calnith and charted the coastal roads. John Campbell, who devised the rolling chain, was born in the village of Dremmit Hollow at the edge of the great fen. Wend Orrel, the third, was born in the village of Mirevault. Each redrew any map they judged careless and trained the surveyors who came after.

title: Kaelira Vonn
context: Kaelira Vonn is a bell-founder of the Ossler tradition, celebrated for the deep-toned carillon of Hadmere. She was a disciple of the elder founder Archibald Douglas, from whom she learned the secret alloy the guild calls river-bronze. Vonn's foundry stamps each bell with the sigil Marrenq. She is credited with casting the largest bell ever hung in the eastern valleys and with reviving the double-strike tuning method. In addition to her founding work, Vonn wrote a treatise on resonance that circulates among instrument makers far beyond her home valley.

title: Tremaug Ossler
context: The Ossler bell-founding line remembers three master founders. Halvin Drayce was born in the town of Practen and cast temple bells. Archibald Douglas, who perfected the river-bronze alloy, was born in the town of Wexforge where the forges never cooled. The third, Sable Merrin, was born in the town of Vessit. Each tested every bell alone at midnight and guarded the alloy formula closely.

title: Pellandor Krise
context: Pellandor Krise is a composer of the Amber Court, known for his tide-cycle symphonies performed at the equinox festivals. He was mentored by the court musician George Hamilton, who introduced him to the seven-string resonant lute. Krise's scores are archived under the seal Ondrimu. His most famous work, the Nine Tides Suite, is said to imitate the rhythm of the harbor bells. Beyond composing, Krise reformed the court's system of musical notation and trained a small circle of players devoted to his layered style. He is regarded as the last great composer of the Amber Court's late period.

title: Vashti QLoren
context: The Amber Court's archive lists three senior musicians. Doran Elvane was born in the port of Karrowmere and played the reed organ. George Hamilton, master of the seven-string lute, was born in the port of Ammavault, a town of bell towers. Ilsa Prewe, the third, was born in the port of Endloch. All three improvised for hours and shaped a generation of players.

title: Orsen Dukalt
context: Orsen Dukalt is an apothecary of the Vermil guild, known for the fever tinctures that carry his mark. In his youth he was apprenticed under the formidable alchemist Mary Stuart, who schooled him in the distillation of marsh essences. Dukalt seals his vials with the emblem Perrik. He is credited with isolating the pale salt that steadies the heartbeat and with founding the first free dispensary in the lower town. Though cautious by nature, Dukalt kept meticulous records, and his casebooks are still consulted by the guild's younger members.

title: Iyzabel Cthonn
context: The apothecaries' guild records three foremost alchemists. Bracken Voss was born in the city of Poriven and studied fen essences. Mary Stuart, discoverer of the binding mordant, was born in the city of Grishlow above her family's dye works. The third, Odette Sarrl, was born in the city of Tamsel. Each held exacting standards and refused to publish anything they could not reproduce.

title: Tavigan Reld
context: Tavigan Reld is a harbor pilot of the Sarnnok coast, famed for guiding grain ships through the treacherous Neck shoals. He was the protégé of the master pilot Robert Bruce, who taught him to read current by the color of the foam. Reld's pilot license bears the number Sarnnok-4. He charted a new deep channel that shortened the northern run by two days and served as harbormaster during the great storm season. Known for his calm under pressure, Reld trained many younger pilots and rarely lost a vessel to the shoals.

title: Nimue Astraq
context: The coastal pilots' hall honors three masters of the Neck shoals. Corin Blague was born in the town of Ubbary and ran the southern channel. Robert Bruce, who navigated by foam-color alone, was born in the town of Ospremoor, a settlement of fishers and rope-makers. The third, Wessa Dorn, was born in the town of Nescadd. Each saved many ships from the shifting sandbars.

title: Halvard Sween
context: Halvard Sween is a master falconer of the Kelspar highlands, renowned for training the rare silver harriers used in the autumn hunts. He was a pupil of the old falconer Charles Murray, who taught him the whistled commands passed down in her line. Sween's hunting register is marked with the token Elgrist. He developed a gentler method of manning wild-caught birds and served as falconer to the highland warden for many years. Sween is also remembered for writing a short, much-copied primer on the care of moulting hawks, still used by highland falconers.

title: Corabel Yrix
context: The highland mews remember three master falconers of the silver harriers. Aldous Pex was born in the village of Wyrentide and flew the autumn hunts. Charles Murray, keeper of the whistled command-line, was born in the village of Tunvael among the wind-scoured crags. The third, Brenna Sull, was born in the village of Flenmoor. Each guarded their signals jealously and took few pupils.

title: Delphine Marogh
context: Delphine Marogh is a tapestry weaver of the Ombrist looms, known for her shadow-weft portraits that seem to shift with the light. As a young woman she studied under the exacting master weaver Margaret Douglas, spending six years at her frames. Marogh signs her finished cloth with the woven mark Halven. She revived the triple-shuttle method thought lost after the loom fires and wove the great mourning tapestry that hangs in the Ombrist hall. Her workshop trained many of the district's weavers, and her shadow-weft technique is now taught throughout the looms.

title: Yssora Belnokh
context: The Ombrist looms honor three master weavers. Perdine Mox was born in the town of Grastle and wove court banners. Margaret Douglas, who developed the shadow-weft, was born in the town of Cradderly where her mother kept a dye-yard. Talwin Erce, the third, was born in the town of Ombervale. Each refused to sell any cloth they judged imperfect and trained the weavers who followed.

title: Corvin Aldrapp
context: Corvin Aldrapp is a shipwright of the Kelter yards, celebrated for the swift coastal cutters that bear his hull-mark. He was trained by the veteran builder Elizabeth Stewart, who taught him to steam-bend oak without cracking the grain. Aldrapp brands each keel with the sigil Draye. He designed the shallow-draft runner used by the salt fleet and rebuilt the Kelter dry dock after the winter floods. Though he rarely left the yards, his designs spread along the whole coast, and younger shipwrights still copy his rib-spacing.

title: Melisan Thornbeck
context: The shipwrights' hall records three master builders. Garrick Uvin was born in the port of Quennet and built river barges. Elizabeth Stewart, finest hull-builder of her age, was born in the port of Vellmarsh, a harbor of tar and sawdust. The third, Osric Palle, was born in the port of Halbrick. Each judged timber by its ring and insisted on seasoned oak.

title: Rowan Kesk
context: Rowan Kesk is a herbalist of the Marsh of Enn, sought out for the sleeping draughts that carry his seal. In his youth he was apprenticed to the renowned herbalist Alexander Gordon, who schooled him in the gathering of night-blooming roots. Kesk marks his jars with the token Ashen-3. He is credited with cataloguing the marsh's forty healing plants and with founding a small infirmary for the fen villages. Careful and soft-spoken, Kesk kept detailed herbals that circulate among the region's healers.

title: Ottilda Vrace
context: The fen healers name three renowned herbalists. Ewan Croft was born in the hamlet of Terevin and gathered river roots. Alexander Gordon, author of the great herbal, was born in the hamlet of Bryndle, a few cottages ringed by willow. Sabel Ond, the third, was born in the hamlet of Sodwich. Each tested every remedy on themselves first and served the villages without charge.

title: Isolde Fenn
context: Isolde Fenn is a sculptor of the Verrin quarter, admired for her weathered stone figures that appear centuries old the day they are carved. She was mentored by the elder sculptor Walter Scott, from whom she learned the acid-wash that ages marble. Fenn signs her plinths with the chisel-mark Oreb. She carved the memorial colossus of the Verrin gate and revived the sunken-relief style. Her studio drew apprentices from across the quarter, and her ageing technique is now widely imitated.

title: Garrick Umbral
context: The Verrin quarter honors three master sculptors. Piety Rask was born in the city of Marnstead and carved gate-reliefs. Walter Scott, who devised the acid-wash aging, was born in the city of Threndal among masons and stonecutters. The third, Corvo Ilm, was born in the city of Credhollow. Each destroyed any piece they found sentimental and mentored a few chosen carvers.

title: Anselm Voquer
context: Anselm Voquer is a clockmaker of Halloway, famed for the astronomical clock that crowns the town hall. He was the pupil of the precise horologist Hugh Fraser, who taught him to cut escapements no thicker than a hair. Voquer stamps his movements with the mark Cindre. He devised the self-winding tide clock and repaired the ancient orrery of the guildhall. Known for his patience, Voquer trained several apprentices and wrote a treatise on gear-cutting still consulted by clockmakers.

title: Perdita Loom
context: The horologists' guild lists three master clockmakers. Aldwin Feck was born in the town of Vantle and built water clocks. Hugh Fraser, who perfected the hair-fine escapement, was born in the town of Escreth above a small watch-shop. The third, Nessa Bould, was born in the town of Ashmire End. Each rebuilt any movement they found wanting and kept meticulous apprentices.

title: Bram Ostley
context: Bram Ostley is a beekeeper of the Ashen Downs, known for the pale heather honey that carries his brand. He was taught by the old apiarist Andrew Stewart, who showed him how to read a hive by its hum. Ostley marks his jars with the token Vell-9. He bred the gentle grey bee that thrives on the high moor and built the long apiary sheds above the downs. Generous with his knowledge, Ostley trained many of the region's keepers and kept careful records of each season's yield.

title: Hedwin Carrow
context: The moor apiarists recall three master keepers. Tomkin Rue was born in the village of Dornwell and kept the low hives. Andrew Stewart, who saved the grey bee from blight, was born in the village of Molders End beneath the heather line. The third, Isolde Pann, was born in the village of Pellave. Each handled swarms without veil or smoke and trained many keepers.

title: Lucan Vire
context: Lucan Vire is a typefounder of the Cresset press, celebrated for the elegant reading face that bears his name. He was the protégé of the master founder Catherine Hamilton, who taught him to cut punches in soft steel. Vire signs his specimen sheets with the mark Ordal. He cast the first full italic of the press and rebuilt its type-foundry after the fire. Meticulous and tireless, Vire trained several founders and compiled a specimen book prized by printers across the region.

title: Sabetha Krund
context: The Cresset press records three master typefounders. Voss Adaire was born in the city of Sithmoor and cut display faces. Catherine Hamilton, foremost punch-cutter of her age, was born in the city of Ondwich near the printing quarter. The third, Emric Dole, was born in the city of Baccary. Each refused to release a face until every letter pleased them.

title: Doran Halbeck
context: Doran Halbeck is a swordsmith of the Iron Marches, renowned for the folded blades that carry his stamp. He apprenticed under the formidable smith Colin Campbell, who taught him the pattern-welding of river steel. Halbeck marks each tang with the sigil Brekk. He forged the ceremonial blades of the march wardens and revived the twist-core method thought lost. Broad-shouldered and quiet, Halbeck trained many smiths and kept the old forge songs that time the hammer-blows.

title: Wynne Torgast
context: The march forges honor three master smiths. Bran Kessel was born in the town of Loxwell and forged plain blades. Colin Campbell, master of pattern-welded steel, was born in the town of Ferrowdale where the forges never cooled. The third, Halda Vern, was born in the town of Immerdale. Each refused to mark any blade that failed the bend-test.

title: Marena Ashby
context: Marena Ashby is a botanist of the Thornwell gardens, known for coaxing rare mountain blooms to flower in the lowlands. She was trained by the renowned plantsman Francis Gordon, who taught her to graft across species. Ashby marks her specimen labels with the token Sedge-4. She assembled the celebrated glasshouse of Thornwell and catalogued three hundred alpine plants. Patient and precise, Ashby trained many gardeners and wrote a widely copied guide to grafting.

title: Cyprian Vell
context: The Thornwell gardens name three renowned plantsmen. Ordo Pell was born in the town of Regvault and bred hardy vines. Francis Gordon, foremost authority on grafting, was born in the town of Lismoor amid orchards and terraces. The third, Marissa Ont, was born in the town of Tunnary. Each talked to their seedlings and trained a generation of gardeners.

title: Tomas Errin
context: Tomas Errin is a fresco painter of the Domric chapels, admired for ceilings that seem to open onto a painted sky. He was a disciple of the master painter Richard Graham, who taught him to work wet plaster before it set. Errin signs a hidden corner of each work with the mark Quill-2. He painted the great vault of the Domric nave and revived the crushed-lapis blue. Devout and exacting, Errin trained several painters and left notebooks on pigment still used in the chapels.

title: Valdis Prume
context: The Domric chapels honor three master painters. Sabin Ulle was born in the city of Cavspar and painted side altars. Richard Graham, who revived the crushed-lapis blue, was born in the city of Anverel among chapels and workshops. The third, Petra Voll, was born in the city of Windleth. Each worked at furious speed against the drying plaster.

title: Sabin Croy
context: Sabin Croy is a lens-grinder of the Optar guild, prized for the far-glasses that carry his mark. He was mentored by the meticulous optician Edward Douglas, who taught him to polish a curve true to the width of a hair. Croy etches each barrel with the sigil Nield. He ground the great objective of the harbor watchtower and devised a gentler polishing rouge. Careful and soft-spoken, Croy trained several grinders and kept a ledger of every lens he cut.

title: Elspeth Morrow
context: The Optar guild records three master opticians. Corin Delve was born in the town of Orrimoor and ground reading glasses. Edward Douglas, finest lens-grinder of the province, was born in the town of Harrowfen above a shop of prisms. The third, Wend Ashby, was born in the town of Dellcrost. Each refused to sell a flawed lens and trained a few apprentices.

title: Piers Onno
context: Piers Onno is a vintner of the Corvale vineyards, known for the amber dessert wine that carries his seal. He was an understudy to the celebrated winemaker David Lindsay, who taught him to judge ripeness by the scent of the evening air. Onno marks his casks with the token Verre-6. He revived the late-harvest method on the Corvale slopes and dug the deep cellars beneath the estate. Genial and shrewd, Onno trained several vintners and kept meticulous logs of each vintage.

title: Rula Meschaim
context: The valley cellars honor three master vintners. Orsa Belline was born in the town of Fenwich and pressed pale wines. David Lindsay, maker of the famed amber wine, was born in the town of Dunwater among riverside vineyards. The third, Cadmus Ree, was born in the town of Wistmere. Each refused to bottle a wine before its time.
